questiontext.text: Which best describes the core mechanism of cocktail shaker sort?

answer.text: Like bubble sort, but it alternates direction each pass — left-to-right, then right-to-left

feedback.text: Correct — bidirectional bubbling moves the largest to the end and the smallest to the front.

answer.text: Divide the array into halves, sort each, then merge

feedback.text: That is merge sort.

answer.text: Build a heap and repeatedly extract the maximum

feedback.text: That is heap sort.
That is shell sort.

generalfeedback.text: Shaker sort is a bidirectional bubble sort: each round bubbles the largest element rightward, then the smallest element leftward.

questiontext.text: What is the worst-case time complexity of shaker sort?

feedback.text: Correct — like bubble sort, it does quadratic work in the worst case.
No — that would require a divide-and-conquer or heap approach.
That is only the best case, on nearly-sorted input.
Far too fast for a comparison-swap bubble variant.

generalfeedback.text: Shaker sort's average and worst cases are O(n^2); its bidirectional passes only offer a constant-factor improvement over plain bubble sort.

questiontext.text: With an early-exit check, what is shaker sort's best-case time on an already-sorted array?

feedback.text: Correct — one pass with no swaps detects sortedness and stops.
That is the worst case, not the best.
No — a single clean pass is linear.
You still must scan all n elements once to confirm order.

generalfeedback.text: Because it can stop when a pass makes no swaps, shaker sort is adaptive: already-sorted input costs only O(n).

feedback.text: Correct — it only swaps adjacent elements when strictly out of order, preserving equal keys' order.
It is stable: adjacent-only swaps never reorder equal keys.

questiontext.text: Shaker sort is an in-place algorithm using only O(1) auxiliary space.

feedback.text: Correct — it swaps within the array with constant extra memory.
Shaker sort needs no auxiliary array; it sorts in place.

questiontext.text: Shaker sort is a bidirectional variant of which basic O(n^2) sort? Answer with one English word.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Small values stuck near the end of the array, which plain bubble sort moves very slowly, are nicknamed ______. Shaker sort mitigates them by also passing right-to-left.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about shaker sort are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It is stable and sorts in place

feedback.text: Yes — adjacent swaps keep it stable, and it needs only O(1) extra space.

answer.text: By passing in both directions it reduces the "turtles" problem of plain bubble sort

feedback.text: Yes — the right-to-left pass moves small values toward the front quickly.

answer.text: Its average-case time is O(n log n)

feedback.text: No — its average case is O(n^2).
No — it is a bubble-sort variant, not divide-and-conquer.

generalfeedback.text: Shaker sort: stable, in-place, adaptive (best O(n)), but average/worst O(n^2) — only a constant-factor gain over bubble sort.
